lead: A lead-acid battery stores energy using lead, lead dioxide and dilute sulfuric acid. A lithium-ion battery shuttles lithium ions between graphite and a metal oxide. Both are secondary cells: discharge is spontaneous, recharge is forced. Lead-acid is cheap and gives high current, so it starts cars and runs inverters and UPS units. Li-ion gives more energy per kilogram, so it powers phones, laptops and electric vehicles. This chapter writes the reactions, compares about 2.1 V per lead-acid cell with about 3.6–3.8 V per Li-ion cell that has a layered oxide cathode such as LiCoO₂, notes that an LiFePO₄ cell gives about 3.2–3.3 V, and explains the six-cell 12 V pack.
prereq: You need: cell EMF and electrode potentials from 4.1, ΔG = −nFE from 4.2, and battery terms from 4.5.

blocks.text: Only a few universities teach this at construction-reaction depth. On discharge, Pb is the negative plate and the anode: oxidation gives electrons. PbO₂ is the positive plate and the cathode: reduction takes electrons. Dilute H₂SO₄ is the electrolyte; a porous separator stops the plates touching but lets ions pass. Each cell gives about 2.1 V; six cells in series give a 12 V battery. Recharge reverses both half-reactions.

blocks.where: Pb is the anode; SO₄²⁻ is sulfate ion; e⁻ is an electron.
PbO₂ is the cathode; H⁺ is hydrogen ion; H₂O is water.
overall discharge; reverse it for recharge.

blocks.text: The key change on discharge is that both plates are converted to lead sulfate (PbSO₄) and the acid is diluted. This is why a discharged cell has weaker acid.

A Li-ion cell uses a graphite anode, a cathode of LiCoO₂ or LiFePO₄, and LiPF₆ salt in an organic solvent. A separator blocks electron contact. Li⁺ ions are intercalated: inserted into layered solids without breaking their structure. On discharge, Li⁺ leaves graphite, crosses the electrolyte, and enters the cathode; electrons go through the load. Charge reverses both flows. One cell gives about 3.6–3.8 V with a layered oxide cathode such as LiCoO₂; an LiFePO₄ cell gives about 3.2–3.3 V.

Advantages: high energy density, low self-discharge, no memory effect. Disadvantages: costly, needs protection circuits, and can catch fire if overcharged or overheated. Under heavy load, internal resistance and polarization cause overvoltage: terminal voltage falls below open-circuit EMF, so less energy reaches the load and heat rises.

Lead-acid is cheap and delivers high surge current, but is heavy and has low energy density. Li-ion is light and energy-dense, but needs careful voltage limits. The electrolyte carries ions, not electrons. This shuttle gives the name rocking-chair battery.

figure.caption: On discharge lithium ions move from graphite through electrolyte to LiCoO₂ while electrons go through the load; charging reverses both flows.

spec.title: Li-ion shuttle
spec.aria: On discharge lithium ions move from graphite anode through electrolyte to lithium cobalt oxide cathode while electrons pass through the load; charge reverses both flows.

examples.question: A lead-acid cell has E = 2.10 V and the cell reaction transfers n = 2 electrons. Find ΔG per cell in J mol⁻¹ and kJ mol⁻¹.
steps: Use ΔG = −nFE. Here n is electrons per reaction, F is Faraday constant 96485 C mol⁻¹, and E is cell EMF 2.10 V.
Apply the sign: ΔG = −405237 J mol⁻¹.
Convert: −405237 ÷ 1000 = −405.237 kJ mol⁻¹, about −405 kJ mol⁻¹.
examples.answer: ΔG = −405,237 J mol⁻¹ = −405.237 kJ mol⁻¹ ≈ −405 kJ mol⁻¹ per cell.
examples.check:
n = 2
F = 96485
E = 2.10
dG = -n * F * E
print(dG)
print(dG / 1000)

traps: A lead-acid cell is about 2.1 V, not 12 V. A 12 V battery has six cells in series.
Do not reverse the discharge reactions when writing recharge; reverse both half-reactions and the overall reaction.
In Li-ion, Li⁺ moves through the electrolyte and electrons move through the external circuit. Do not send electrons through the electrolyte.
PbO₂ is the cathode on discharge, not the anode. Pb is oxidized.
3.6–3.8 V is per Li-ion cell with a layered oxide cathode, not per pack. LiFePO₄ cells give about 3.2–3.3 V.

quiz.q: Write the overall discharge reaction of a lead-acid cell.
Why does a 12 V lead-acid battery use six cells?
quiz.a: Each cell gives about 2.1 V; series connection adds voltages, so six give about 12.6 V.

quiz.q: A Li-ion cell is 3.7 V. How many series cells give about 11.1 V?
Why does a battery's terminal voltage fall under heavy load?
quiz.a: Internal resistance drops IR volts and polarization adds a further voltage drop. V_terminal = EMF − I·R_internal − V_polarization, where R_internal is in ohms, I is the current in amperes and V_polarization is the polarization (overvoltage) in volts. A large current lowers terminal voltage and wastes heat.

quiz.q: What is intercalation in a Li-ion cell?
quiz.a: Li⁺ ions enter or leave layered electrode solids without destroying the host structure.

quiz.q: For a cell with E = 2.05 V and n = 2, find ΔG.

beyond: Not for the exam. Battery management systems track cell voltage and temperature; thermal-runaway modelling and lithium recycling are active areas. Solid-state and sodium-ion cells aim at safety and lower cost. Search for intercalation chemistry, SEI layer and lead-acid recycling.
